I want to make your website incredible.

I'm Adam Cornell. My day job is at AugustAsh; my side work is Ashen Rayne, which I run with my best bud of about 30 years, Cyle Carlson. He works at AugustAsh too, and he's on that page. We've both been there 16 years or so: he leads the development team, and I lead the support team.

You'd be working with Ashen Rayne.

There's no salesman here. I'm the developer who built this concept, I'm the one writing this note, and I'd build the whole site. This is how I find work: I come across a site, think “I want to rebuild that”, and I try to make it happen. Yes, I make good money doing this, and I should: I'm good at it. However, I'm mainly here because I love cars, I like the essence of Ferrari, and I love racing: I love corners.

I've seen your ads in FORZA for a while, but I'd never looked at the website until last week, when I read “Progression”, Colin's story in issue 227 (yes, I'm a little behind in my reading). A company small in size, big in stature, run by a racer: that's a business I'd like to work with. And a site that sells Ferrari parts? Let me at it.

So I started where your customers already meet you, with your magazine ad. I like it, and you must've liked it too, so I twisted it a little. The sky reminded me of space, and space, Ferrari, technology: it all makes sense. What's cooler than that?

What's below is built to give you the feel of what I'm aiming at, with some working previews. I don't do a badrillion mockups and have you analyse every little thing. I send you a preview and ask: do you like it? Then I migrate your existing site into the new one, and do a bunch of wizardry along the way to make it better.

The last site I built was dmx-power.com: a very old site migrated into a new one, and the old site was… not great. I still have the old site's dev environment running, so you can see the before next to the after. It may take a minute to load: dev environments go to sleep, and your visit wakes it up.

My contact details are in the signature of the email this came with. I generally ignore phone calls (I get so much spam), so email or text me and then we'll get on the phone.

I'm actually pumped about what I've built here. I've been through a lot of parts sites, because I do all my own work on my cars. I currently have a '14 Maserati Ghibli S Q4, and my wife is in an Audi S5 (she has a lead foot). She won't quite listen to me about lines, though (can't win 'em all). On mine: cats removed, titanium exhaust, tune. I've been hooking AI up to my car through the OBD port and experimenting with tuning too. It's interesting…

Back to the point: I love the search, vehicle first (and it's slick) and then straight into parts, and the car modelling. You can literally click on the centre console of the model and see all the parts in that zone. It's so fast, so good, so cool. I was showing Kellie (my wife) last night because I thought it was so awesome. Ok, ok, I'll shut up.

The red ? markers explain how a piece would be built. Everything else is the site as your customers would see it.

Your car, then your part

No menus to climb and no grid of models to hunt through. Type your car the way you'd say it and pick it from a short list. The same box then searches parts, and only the parts that fit come back. Pick the car once and the whole site follows: every search, every price, every drawing. This concept carries the F355, every part your site lists for it.

Try a car

Then a part?

Say it your way

355 spider is enough. No make, no menu, no knowing which group a model lives in. Nicknames work too: Daytona, Boxer, QV.

The year picks the version

97 355 spider lands on the 5.2 Motronic. Years can be short: 87, not 1987.

Options, once

Steering side, the market it was built for, power steering, air con, chassis, engine and gearbox numbers. Guessed from the country where they can be, asked once, saved with the car. Parts that depend on them sort themselves.

Your garage

The cars you've picked wait at the top next time. Two cars in the family or the shop? Each is one tap away.

A number needs no car

Type a part number, or an old superseded one, into either box and go straight to the part.

Then the part

Numbers, old numbers, six languages, or plain words like left driver axle. A broad search offers the words that narrow it, and the plus on each result puts it in the basket.

The car decides, not the customer

Some parts change partway through a model's life. The F355's alternator belt changed at chassis #31228; the clutch flanges changed at gearbox #2439 and again at #2716. Today that's a note in brackets, and the customer reads it and hopes. The new site knows the car's numbers, or works them out, and shows the part that fits.

Try it

Only what fits

Once the site knows the car's number, the customer sees only the belt that fits. Until then the two share one card, each labelled with its chassis range, so nothing is guessed.

Enter it, and it's a check

Chassis, engine and gearbox numbers live in the car's options. With them, anything outside the car's numbers is hidden, and anything already in the basket that doesn't match is flagged before checkout.

Leave it blank, and it learns

Choose the later belt and the site knows the car is #31228 or later. Each ranged part after that narrows it further, from either end. A part for cars with power steering answers that question too. The options show what it has learned, with a way to forget it.

When it can't tell, it asks

A part that depends on something the site doesn't know says so, with a link. It opens the car's options full-screen with that field lit; save, and the customer is back where they were, now seeing only what fits.

Never past the evidence

A choice that disagrees with what it knows doesn't move the range; the basket asks the customer to check. If a part depends on which of two gearboxes the car has and that isn't known, nothing is assumed.

Already in your listings

Your pages already say it: Up to Chassis #31227, Valid from gearbox Nr. 2439 and till Nr. 2715, Valid until engine #37561. On the F355 alone, 17 parts carry a range. The site reads them as data instead of small print. In the build they become fields on the part, set once by your team, and every model's ranges work the same way.

Every part, on the car

Your parts are already filed by section and heading, and named left and right: Body Panels, Exhaust, Suspension bushes (rear), LH Rear Diffuser. That is enough for the site to place each part on a drawing of the car by itself, with nobody drawing it in. Of the 1,816 rows on your F355 pages, 1,564 find their place this way. Manuals and brochures go in the glovebox, clothing on the driver. The rest are tools, stickers and loose fixings, which belong nowhere on the car.

It picks its own view

A door lights the door. A diffuser turns the car over. A cam belt opens the engine. Everything else steps out of the way.

No words to translate

The drawing reads the same in all six languages, and the steering wheel sits on the side the customer drives from.

One drawing, every car

Each model is a few measurements and its layout: where the engine sits and which way it lies, the gearbox, the drive. Dino to FF, Fiat and Lancia, from the one drawing.

Point at the car

Click any part of the car to see everything you sell for it.

The driver and the glovebox

Not everything you sell bolts on, and it still gets a place in the car. Owner's manuals, workshop manuals, yearbooks and brochures are in the glovebox. Jackets, gloves and caps are on the driver, sat in their seat in a helmet, on whichever side the customer drives from. Click either and it all comes up.

What a customer runs into today

The site was built when hand-made pages and a hosted basket were how a specialist sold online, and it has carried a very large catalogue a long way: your team keeps thousands of parts, prices and fitments current by hand. What follows is the gap between what was right then and what's possible now.

Finding a part

Now

The 308 Engine General page is one page of 335 parts under 49 headings, with 748 pictures. Before it finishes loading it has asked for more than 3.6 MB.

Next

Type what you're after: a part number, an old number, a name in your own language, or the car and the part. The results are the filter, and a phone loads only what it shows. It works above.

Search

Now

The search box hands the question to Google, which answers with pages. Search for 105206, the 308 timing belt tensioner bearing, and it offers 23 pages to scroll through.

Next

Search answers with parts: by number, by the number it superseded, by name in the customer's language, with the right one for their car first.

On a phone

Now

Pages are laid out 1,045 pixels wide with nothing telling a phone how to show them, so a phone shrinks the desktop page to fit.

Next

Built for the phone first, the way most people now shop, and still at home on a workshop desktop.

Postage

Now

Postage is worked out after the order is packed and added before the card is charged, so a customer abroad orders without knowing the total.

Next

Rates at checkout, live from Royal Mail, Parcelforce and FedEx, with freight quoted for the big pieces. See how.

One part, one price

Now

A part that fits several cars is typed onto each of their pages, with its price typed each time. On just the five pages in this concept, 146 of 868 rows repeat a part number listed elsewhere.

Next

Each part is entered once, with every car it fits. Change its price once and every page that lists it agrees.

Languages

Now

Google's widget translates a page in the visitor's browser, after it arrives. Search engines only ever see the English.

Next

Each language gets its own pages, translated once and checked, so a German enthusiast searching for a Zahnriemen can find yours. See how.

A page for every part

Now

A part lives as a row on a long page. It has no address of its own, so it can't be shared, bookmarked, or found on its own in Google.

Next

This is SEO work. Every part gets a page with its own address, photo, fitment and price, written so a search for its part number can land on it. Open any part above to see one.

Pictures

Now

Each part photo is one 500-pixel JPEG, many over 100 KB, sent from your own server at about half a second apiece before it starts, and marked so no cache along the way can keep it. A shelf of manuals fills in one picture at a time.

Next

Bigger pictures, made from your original photos rather than the 500-pixel copies: sharp on today's high-density screens, with a zoom on the part's page. Each is made at the size it shows, in a modern format, and served from close to the customer. Nobody resizes anything by hand.

On the shelf

Now

The site can't see your shelves. A few parts say "Currently on Manufacturer Back Order", typed in by hand; for the rest, a customer finds out a part is out of stock after they've ordered it.

Next

Every part shows where it stands, read from wherever your stock already lives: on the shelf and dispatched today, due on a date, or on back order. Nobody types it. One for you: when a part is on back order and a kit contains it, should the kit be unavailable too?

After the order

Now

The basket is a separate hosted service with no link to your stock, your customers or your accounts, so your team carries every web order across by hand.

Next

A web order lands in the system you already run, like a phone order would, with the customer and payment attached. Or, if that system frustrates you or costs a fortune every year, the new site can become it. More on that below.

Counting visits

Now

The site still carries Google's old Universal Analytics, which stopped recording visits in July 2023.

Next

Analytics that know it's a shop: what people search for and don't find, which parts they look at, and where a basket stops.

Their language, their currency

Your ad says it: we supply parts to the USA and across the world. The new site would greet each customer in their own language, price in their currency, and be found by the searches they type at home.

One part, six languages ?

Each language has its own address, so search engines index it, and a German search for the part finds the German page.

    01Written onceYour team writes or edits the part in English, as now.
    02TranslatedA translation service drafts each language, using your own glossary of part names.

    04PublishedEach language updates on its own, without clearing the rest of the site.

    Found in America

    In the US, Superformance is also the name of a Florida car maker, and it owns superformance.com. A US buyer searching your name meets theirs first.

    It's worth winning. As you told FORZA, you carry parts American aftermarket sellers often can't, so a US buyer who finds you has usually found the part.

    Still one site

    This is SEO work, and it stays one site with one checkout. US English is simply one more language, like German or Italian. The same pages carry US spelling, US part names and dollar prices, and they're marked so Google shows them to US searchers.

    • Live rates from your carriersRoyal Mail, Parcelforce and FedEx, priced from each part's weight and size, for the address the customer types.
    • Weights, close enough to startLive rates need each part's weight and size, and your site doesn't hold them today. If your stock system already does, the site reads them from there. If not, every part starts with a sensible estimate for its kind: a washer, a brake disc, a bumper, a crankshaft. Your team corrects the big and awkward ones, and the weights from real parcels sharpen the rest over time. Close is fine for a parcel; anything heavy enough to matter goes to freight.
    • More than one shelfIf parts sit in different warehouses, or some ship direct from a supplier, the site works out a dispatch date that allows for gathering them. Your customer sees one estimated, honest date; the routing stays on your side.
    • Freight, without the guessworkA crated engine block or a set of body panels asks for a quote instead of a rate. The customer gets one, by email, and pays from it.
    • Charged when it ships, as nowCards are authorised at the order and charged at dispatch, the way you work today, through Stripe. Apple Pay, Google Pay and Amazon Pay come with it.
    • Accounts, for the tradeWorkshops, restorers and Ferrari dealers already buy from you, and your contact form asks for an account number. Their accounts become users on the site, and users can be grouped into organisations, so a workshop's whole team sits under one account. Each organisation can carry its own price handling: where it follows a rule, like a percentage off or a trade band, the site does the maths, and whoever signs in sees their own price on every page, in search and at checkout. They'd also get their order history, paste a list of part numbers straight from a job sheet, and reorder in two clicks.

    Made, sourced and checked by Superformance

    The parts your customers can't get anywhere else are your best story. When the factory can no longer supply a part for an older car, Ferrari's own dealers come to you. Today those parts are rows in a list like any other. The new site gives them their own place.

      How we'd build it

      Your catalogue is the hard part, and you've already built it. The new site carries it across and gives it the shop it deserves.

      Every part, carried across

      Every model page read in, every part entered once with every car it fits, duplicates merged by part number, nothing retyped.

      Old links still land

      Each current page and bookmark forwards to its new home, so nothing your customers or Google know about breaks.

      A shop, not a link

      A real basket, checkout and order history, payments through Stripe, and joined to the system your stock and accounts already live in.

      Search that knows parts

      Part numbers, superseded numbers, fitment and names in every language, with spelling forgiven.

      Your team edits it

      A new part is a photo and a few fields. Its pages, its search and its translations follow on their own.

      Fast everywhere

      Each language and currency served from cache close to the customer, refreshed only where something changed.

      A private full build, on a development site of its own. You use it, we adjust, and it goes live when you're happy.

      After launch

      Once the shop is live, I'm still around: monthly updates and maintenance, here to fix and address issues, and here to combine our imaginations to make everything even more awesome.
